title: Shemini: grief has its reasons (Leviticus 10:16–20)
hookLine: Aaron doesn't eat the offering in his grief; Moses hears him out and agrees

cards: A manager notices a missed deadline and walks over, ready to say something sharp. Then the employee says, quietly: my father died on Tuesday. The manager has a choice.
Hold the line, because rules are rules, or hear the reason, and let it change the answer. The same afternoon Aaron lost his sons, there was still work to do in the sanctuary.
One offering was supposed to be eaten by the priests. It wasn't. It was burned instead.
And Moses, who has just lost two nephews himself, goes looking for it.

teach.b: Moses searches. The Hebrew says darosh darash, he searched and searched, for the goat of the sin offering, and finds it burned.
He's angry, and he aims it at Aaron's two surviving sons, Elazar and Itamar: why didn't you eat it in the holy place, as I commanded?
An old scribal tradition, recorded in the Talmud, counts darosh darash as the middle words of the whole Torah. The center of the scroll is a man searching.
Then Aaron answers for his sons, speaking for the first time since the fire. In plain words: today they brought their offerings, and today such things have happened to me.
If I had eaten the sin offering today, would that have been good in God's eyes? He doesn't argue the law.
He names his grief, and asks whether a mourner's meal is the kind of holiness God wants.

teach.h: MOSES HEARS, AND IT WAS GOOD.
teach.b: And Moses hears. The text says that when Moses heard, it was good in his eyes. Rashi adds the striking part: Moses admitted it, and wasn't ashamed to say, I hadn't heard that rule.
The lawgiver, on that terrible day, says in effect: you're right, and I was wrong.

teach.h: THE LAW MAKES ROOM FOR MOURNERS.
teach.b: Commentators draw a lesson: a law can make room for a mourner, and the one who holds authority can change course after listening.
Jewish law still does this: a mourner before the funeral is exempt from many commandments, so the grief can be what it is.

how: In Jewish law a mourner between a death and the burial, an onen, is exempt from many positive commandments, and during shiva the community brings food and leads prayers in the mourner's home so the mourner can simply grieve.

o: a mourner: one who has just lost family
eighth: the portion where grief meets law
searched: what Moses did for the offering

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: searched for the goat of the offering
asked: would eating today be good?

s: Moses insisted the rule be kept
when he heard Aaron's answer, it was good in his eyes.
darosh darash is counted as the middle of the Torah's words
an old scribal count recorded in the Talmud puts the center there.
a mourner before the funeral keeps every commandment as usual
Jewish law exempts the onen from many commandments.

games.q: you're Moses. the offering that should have been eaten was burned, and Aaron says: after what happened to me today, would eating it have been good? what do you do?
o: insist the law is the law.
games.why: Moses heard, and it was good in his eyes. Rashi says he wasn't ashamed to admit he'd been wrong.

practice: Think of someone you love who is carrying something heavy, and handling it differently than you would: too quiet, too busy, too angry, too much.

If a rule in you says they're doing it wrong, notice it; then, like Moses, hear their reason, even if you have to imagine it, and let it be good in your eyes. If you pray, hold them in your prayers just as they are.

wordCard.voice: Shemini, the eighth: the portion where Aaron, in his grief, doesn't eat the offering, and Moses listens, and agrees.

orig.note: Hebrew: "and it was good in his eyes": how Moses took Aaron's answer.

carryVoice: Your line: Moses heard, and agreed. Listening first changed the whole answer. Day three hundred ninety-three.
